name: Wakan Tanka
description: Wakan Tanka (Great Mystery or Great Spirit) is the supreme sacred power in Lakota religion, the unified totality of all that is mysterious, powerful, and sacred. Unlike a personified deity in Western traditions, Wakan Tanka is better understood as the sum of all wakan (sacred) forces that permeate the universe. The term encompasses four primary deities: Wi (Sun), Skan (Sky), Maka (Earth), and Inyan (Rock), along with their associates. Everything in creation possesses wakan energy as part of Wakan Tanka.
appearance: Not depicted in physical form, Wakan-Tanka is understood as the Great Mystery encompassing all of creation. When represented symbolically, it appears as the sun, the sky, or the vast expanse of the cosmos, containing all things within its infinite being.
behavior: The supreme creative force and universal spirit in Lakota belief, encompassing all aspects of the sacred. Wakan-Tanka is not a single personified deity but the sum of all sacred powers. All things — the earth, the sky, the animals, and humans — are part of this one great mystery.
habitat: Omnipresent—exists throughout the universe and within all creation
cultural_significance: The central concept of Lakota religion, often equated with the Great Spirit. Represented the sacred energy underlying all existence, from which all deities and spirits emanate.
summary: The supreme sacred power and creative force in Lakota religion
fun_fact: Wakan Tanka is not a single personified deity but rather the unified totality of all sacred powers in the universe, with four primary manifestations: Wi (Sun), Skan (Sky), Maka (Earth), and Inyan (Rock)
seo_description: Wakan Tanka (Great Mystery or Great Spirit) is the supreme sacred power in Lakota religion, the unified totality of all that is mysterious, powerful,
source: Wikipedia / Black Elk / Walker's Lakota Belief and Ritual

name: Unhcegila
description: Unhcegila (Unk Cekula) is a gigantic serpentoid creature from Lakota mythology responsible for many unexplained disappearances and deaths. Described as a massive dragon-like serpent with impenetrable scales, eyes of fire, and a fanged mouth shrouded in smoke or cloud. Her only weakness was a seventh spot on her body where her heart lay burning within. She emerged from primordial waters, was fought by the Thunderbird Wakinyan, and her shattered bones became the Badlands. Various heroes—a Bear Clan warrior guided by Weasel, or two brothers with medicine arrows—defeated her by cutting their way out from inside or striking her heart spot.
appearance: Massive serpentine body with impenetrable dark scales, eyes of fire, fanged mouth shrouded in smoky cloud, iron-like claws, voice like thunder. May have horns. Her body is covered in nearly impenetrable scales.
behavior: A monstrous horned serpent that dwells in deep waters, lakes, and rivers. It is a malevolent and destructive force that drags people and animals underwater to drown them. It can cause floods and earthquakes, and its presence poisons the water. It is associated with chaos and the underworld.
habitat: Primordial waters, lakes, rivers, the Black Hills, later her bones became the Badlands
weaknesses: seventh spot on torso where heart lies
loses power if tail is severed
cultural_significance: Explains the geological formations of the Badlands and the sacred red pipestone quarry. Her defeat by various heroes demonstrates Lakota values of courage, spiritual guidance, and cooperation.
summary: Gigantic serpent monster from Lakota mythology whose bones became the Badlands
fun_fact: Unhcegila's only weakness was a seventh spot on her body hiding her burning heart; one account says the Thunderbird Wakinyan killed her with lightning, scattering her bones to form the Badlands
seo_description: Unhcegila (Unk Cekula) is a gigantic serpentoid creature from Lakota mythology responsible for many unexplained disappearances and deaths. Described a
source: Wikipedia / Native American Mythology A to Z

name: Inyan
description: Inyan (Rock) is the oldest of all beings in Lakota creation mythology. He existed at the very beginning alongside Wakan Tanka the Great Mystery and the darkness Han. Inyan wished to exercise his powers of compassion, so he sacrificed much of his own substance to create Maka (the Earth), giving his blood which became all the waters of the world. In doing so he shriveled, became hard, and lost his powers. He is the grandfather of all things and one of the four primary Wakan Tanka deities.
appearance: The primordial rock, the first being created in Lakota cosmology. Inyan is depicted as an enormous, ancient stone formation that contains all potential within its solid form. It is dark, hard, and timeless, representing the foundational substance of the universe.
behavior: Originally, Inyan was all-powerful and fluid like water, but he sacrificed his power and fluidity to create Maka (the Earth). He gave up his blood to create the waters of the world and became the hard, silent rock that forms the foundation of all existence.
habitat: The earth, embedded in soil—Skan decreed rock and soil must remain bound together
weaknesses: shriveled and lost most of his power after creating Maka
cultural_significance: Central figure in the Lakota creation narrative, representing the ultimate sacrifice for creation. Explains why rocks are embedded in soil across the landscape.
summary: Primordial rock deity who sacrificed himself to create the Earth in Lakota mythology
fun_fact: Inyan created Maka (the Earth) from his own body, sacrificing his blood which became the waters, and shriveled into the hard rocks we see today
seo_description: Inyan (Rock) is the oldest of all beings in Lakota creation mythology. He existed at the very beginning alongside Wakan Tanka the Great Mystery and th
source: Wikipedia / Lakota mythology

name: Maka
description: Maka is the Earth goddess in Lakota mythology, created by Inyan from his own substance. She is the grandmother of all things and one of the four primary Wakan Tanka deities. She complained of cold and darkness, leading Inyan to create Anpo (Dawn) and Wi (Sun). When she tried to separate herself from Inyan, Skan ruled that rock and soil must remain bound together, explaining why rocks are embedded in the earth. She provides food, clothing, and shelter to all living beings.
appearance: The Earth Mother, depicted as a nurturing woman with dark skin that resembles rich soil, her hair flowing like prairie grass. She wears a gown of green fields and autumn leaves, and her eyes reflect the deep wisdom of the land itself.
behavior: Created by Inyan's sacrifice, Maka became the earth beneath all living things. She is both the literal ground and a living spirit, supporting all life upon her surface. She represents the feminine principle of stability, fertility, and nurturing in Lakota cosmology.
habitat: The earth—all land, plains, mountains, and soil
cultural_significance: Represents the earth as grandmother and mother in Lakota religion. Associated with sustenance, agriculture, and the material foundation of life.
summary: Earth goddess and grandmother of all things in Lakota mythology
fun_fact: Maka tried to separate herself from Inyan after creation, but Skan ruled that rock and soil must stay bound—which is why rocks are embedded in the earth
seo_description: Maka is the Earth goddess in Lakota mythology, created by Inyan from his own substance. She is the grandmother of all things and one of the four prima
source: Wikipedia / Lakota mythology

name: Skan
description: Skan (Taku Skanskan) is the sky spirit and supreme judge of the universe in Lakota mythology. He was created from the waters that could not retain Inyan's powers. He gives life and motion to all things and serves as the ultimate arbitrator of cosmic disputes. When Maka appealed to him to separate from Inyan, Skan decreed they must remain bound. He judges souls after death and determines the fate of spirits. He is one of the four primary Wakan Tanka deities and associated with the color blue of the sky.
appearance: The blue sky itself, though as a spirit what humans see is only his visible aspect. He is omnipresent as the sky that covers all things, formless yet everywhere at once. When manifesting, he appears as a vast, luminous blue presence stretching from horizon to horizon.
behavior: The supreme judge and giver of life and motion to all things. He resolves disputes among the gods and judges the souls of the dead. He is associated with health, strength, and the sky domain. As the ultimate arbiter, his decisions are final and unquestionable in the Lakota spiritual hierarchy.
cultural_significance: One of the four primary Wakan Tanka deities, representing divine justice, judgment, and the life-giving force that animates all creation.
summary: Sky spirit and supreme judge of the universe in Lakota mythology
fun_fact: Skan was created when Inyan's blood became water that could not retain his powers; Skan became the supreme judge who rules on cosmic disputes and judges departed souls
seo_description: Skan (Taku Skanskan) is the sky spirit and supreme judge of the universe in Lakota mythology. He was created from the waters that could not retain Iny
source: Wikipedia / Walker's Lakota Belief and Ritual

name: Anpo
description: Anpo (Anpao) is the spirit of dawn in Lakota mythology, created by Inyan to bring light to Maka when she complained of cold and darkness. Anpo's red light illuminated the world, but it was not enough for Maka, leading to the creation of Wi the Sun. Later, when Maka complained of being too hot, Skan decreed that Han (darkness) and Anpo should follow each other around the world, creating the cycle of day and night. Anpo represents the first light of creation, the transition from darkness to illumination.
appearance: The dawn light personified, appearing as a soft, golden radiance that spreads across the eastern sky each morning. Anpo is the first light of creation, a warm glow that illuminates the world gradually, bringing sight and clarity to all beings who await the new day.
behavior: The first light created to dispel the darkness of the primordial world. Anpo prepares the way for Wi the sun, heralding the day with gentle illumination. As the dawn, Anpo represents hope, new beginnings, and the daily renewal of life.
habitat: The eastern sky at dawn, associated with the horizon
weaknesses: his light alone was not sufficient for Maka
cultural_significance: Represents the creation of light and the daily cycle of day and night in Lakota cosmology.
summary: Spirit of dawn who brought the first light to creation in Lakota mythology
fun_fact: Anpo was created when Maka complained of cold and darkness; his red light was insufficient so Inyan created Wi the Sun afterward
seo_description: Anpo (Anpao) is the spirit of dawn in Lakota mythology, created by Inyan to bring light to Maka when she complained of cold and darkness. Anpo's red l
source: Wikipedia / Lakota mythology

name: Wi
description: Wi is the Sun god in Lakota mythology, created by Inyan to provide sufficient warmth and light for Maka after Anpo's dawn light proved inadequate. Wi is one of the four primary Wakan Tanka deities and is considered above all other Wakan Tanka in some traditions. He is associated with the supreme power of creation and receives prayers for matters of great importance. In some accounts, Wi is identified as Wakan Tanka Kin (the Great Spirit) itself. The Sun gives life to all growing things and marks the passage of time.
appearance: The sun in the sky, brilliant, life-giving, and all-seeing. Wi is one of the four primary Wakan Tanka manifestations, appearing as a blazing disc of light that travels across the heavens daily, his warmth sustaining all life on the earth below.
behavior: Provides light, warmth, and life to the world. He receives prayers of the highest importance through Wohpe the mediator. He governs the daily cycle and is considered the highest of the Wakan Tanka in some Lakota traditions, with the most sacred prayers carried directly to him.
weaknesses: sets at night (half the time in the sky)
cultural_significance: One of the four primary Wakan Tanka deities, representing the supreme life-giving power of the sun. Central to Lakota cosmology and prayer.
summary: Sun god and one of the four primary Wakan Tanka deities in Lakota mythology
fun_fact: Wi is considered the highest of the Wakan Tanka in some Lakota traditions—prayers of great importance are carried directly to the Sun through the mediator Wohpe
seo_description: Wi is the Sun god in Lakota mythology, created by Inyan to provide sufficient warmth and light for Maka after Anpo's dawn light proved inadequate. Wi
source: Wikipedia / Walker's Lakota Belief and Ritual

name: Ksapela
description: Ksapela (Little Wisdom) is a minor spirit in Lakota mythology, also known as Gnaski. He is the son of Iya (the destructive storm monster) and Unk (the spirit of contention). Ksapela managed to outwit and perfectly mimic Ksa (the spirit of wisdom) to the point that the two were indistinguishable, earning him the name 'little wisdom.' He appears in the Great Race story as the wise one who proposed the competition between the four-legged animals and the two-legged birds to determine who would eat whom.
appearance: A wise old spirit with the features of an ancient Lakota elder, with long gray hair, deep-set eyes full of ancient knowledge, and a weathered face marked by countless years. He carries a staff carved with symbols representing the accumulated wisdom of the ages.
behavior: The embodiment of wisdom and intelligence in Lakota cosmology. He represents the power of knowledge and the importance of careful thought. He guides those who seek understanding and punishes those who act without thinking. He is invoked by those who need wise counsel.
weaknesses: imperfect mimicry—ultimately distinguishable from true wisdom
cultural_significance: Represents false wisdom and cunning, provides moral lessons about the difference between true knowledge and clever mimicry.
summary: Spirit of mimicry and false wisdom in Lakota mythology
fun_fact: Ksapela outwitted Ksa the spirit of wisdom by perfectly mimicking him until even the gods could not tell them apart

name: Hihankara
description: Hihankara (Owl-Maker) is an aged owl spirit in Lakota mythology who stands at the entrance to the Milky Way—the path of the dead. She judges the souls (nagi) of the deceased who ascend the Sky-Road after death. Those who bear the proper sacred tattoos are admitted to the happy hunting ground; those without proper tattoos are pushed back to Earth to wander as restless ghosts or are removed from existence entirely. She represents the transition between life and the afterlife.
appearance: The great horned owl spirit, appearing as a massive owl with piercing golden eyes and prominent ear tufts. Its feathers are mottled brown and white, and it moves with silent, ghostly grace through the darkness. Its hoot is deep and resonant, carrying wisdom on the night air.
behavior: The guardian of the night who protects sleepers and watches over the darkness. Associated with wisdom and clear seeing in the dark, Hihankara guides those who must navigate difficult times. The owl's ability to see in darkness symbolizes spiritual vision and hidden knowledge.
habitat: The entrance to the Milky Way (Sky-Road), the spirit path to the afterlife
weaknesses: can be satisfied by proper tattoos and spiritual preparation
cultural_significance: Hihankara represents the Lakota belief in judgment after death and the importance of proper spiritual preparation and ritual markings during life.
summary: Owl spirit who judges souls at the entrance to the Milky Way in Lakota mythology
fun_fact: Hihankara examines every deceased soul that ascends the Milky Way; those without proper tattoos are denied entry to the happy hunting ground
seo_description: Hihankara (Owl-Maker) is an aged owl spirit in Lakota mythology who stands at the entrance to the Milky Way—the path of the dead. She judges the souls
source: Wikipedia / Lakota oral tradition

name: Buffalo Spirit
description: The Buffalo Spirit (Tatanka) is one of the most powerful and revered animal spirits in Lakota mythology. The buffalo is considered a relative of the Lakota people and a source of life, providing food, clothing, shelter, and tools. Buffalo spirits appear in many stories—as the buffalo people who intermarry with humans, as spirit guides in vision quests, and as the ultimate gift from the Creator. The White Buffalo Calf Woman is the most sacred manifestation of the buffalo spirit. The buffalo also appears as one of the Wakan Kuya (lesser sacred beings).
appearance: A great buffalo bull or cow, majestic and powerful with a massive dark coat and horns that span wide. May appear in spirit form as a buffalo-shaped being of golden light or in human form as a buffalo person wearing a horned headdress and robe of buffalo hide.
behavior: Protector and provider for the Lakota people, teaching respect for the hunt and proper ceremony. He appears in visions to grant spiritual power and can take human form to instruct the people. He is a Wakan Kuya (lesser sacred being) but holds immense spiritual significance.
habitat: The Great Plains, the spirit world, sacred sites
weaknesses: hunting without respect offends the buffalo spirit
cultural_significance: Central to Lakota spirituality—the buffalo provided everything the Lakota needed to survive and thrives as a spiritual relative.
summary: Sacred buffalo spirit that provides for and protects the Lakota people
fun_fact: The Buffalo spirit is so central to Lakota life that it is classified as one of the Wakan Kuya (lesser sacred beings), and the White Buffalo Calf Woman is its holiest manifestation
seo_description: The Buffalo Spirit (Tatanka) is one of the most powerful and revered animal spirits in Lakota mythology. The buffalo is considered a relative of the L
source: Lakota oral tradition / Black Elk

name: Apistotoke
description: Apistotoke (also known as Ihtsipatapiyohpa, 'Source of Life') is the great creator god of the Blackfoot people. A divine spirit with no human form or attributes, Apistotoke is entirely gender-neutral and never personified in traditional folklore. He created the Sky Beings (Naato'si the Sun, Ko'komiki'somm the Moon, and the stars), then Ksahkomitapi (Earth) as mother to all creation. Na'pi (Old Man) was created as the first man and demigod who shaped the world. Apistotoke takes a minimal role in folklore, with Na'pi and Kipitaakii performing the hands-on work of creation and teaching.
appearance: The Supreme Being and creator in Blackfoot mythology, often depicted as an abstract, formless power that is the source of all existence. When represented, Apistotoke appears as a wise elder with flowing white hair, wrapped in a star-studded blanket that contains all of creation.
behavior: Created the world and everything in it from the primordial waters. He is the ultimate source of power and authority in the Blackfoot spiritual system. He delegated authority to the Sun and other spirits but remains the supreme power. He is merciful and just, the foundation of Blackfoot spirituality.
habitat: The heavens, the spirit realm—too great to be directly approached except through prayer with the sacred pipe
cultural_significance: The supreme creator of the Blackfoot people, equated with the Christian God in modern times. Represents the ultimate source of all life and creation.
summary: Great creator god of the Blackfoot people, source of all life and creation
fun_fact: Apistotoke is entirely gender-neutral in original Blackfoot texts despite being described as male in modern English translations; the name literally means 'Our Creator.'

source: Wikipedia / Native-Languages.org / Blackfoot oral tradition

name: Na'pi
description: Na'pi (Old Man) is the primary culture hero, creator figure, and trickster of Blackfoot mythology. Created by Apistotoke as the first man and demigod, Na'pi shaped the world using mud brought by Turtle during a great flood. He created humans from clay, taught the Blackfoot which plants to eat and animals to hunt, and introduced buffalo. Na'pi is simultaneously wise creator and foolish trickster—he made the land, established the seasons, gave people fire, but also gets into endless trouble through greed, pride, and foolishness. His adventures include the rolling skull, the mossy rock, stealing summer, and the creation of death (when Kipitaakii threw a stone instead of wood into the river).
appearance: An old man with a wrinkled, weathered face, a long gray beard, and a mischievous twinkle in his eyes. He dresses in simple Blackfoot clothing and carries a walking stick. Despite his aged appearance, he moves with surprising quickness and agility.
behavior: The creator-trickster who shaped the world but whose foolishness caused many problems. He created humans and animals, taught essential skills, but also introduced death and suffering through his mistakes. He is both revered as a culture hero and laughed at as a bumbling fool.
habitat: The Blackfoot territory (Montana, Alberta), the plains, mountains
weaknesses: greed and pride cause his plans to fail
cultural_significance: Central figure in Blackfoot culture—explains the origins of landscape, seasons, animals, death, and social customs. His stories are among the most beloved in Blackfoot tradition.
summary: Primary culture hero and trickster of Blackfoot mythology who shaped the world and taught humans
fun_fact: Na'pi determined human mortality when his wife Kipitaakii threw a stone instead of a piece of wood into the river—the sinking stone decreed permanent death
seo_description: Na'pi (Old Man) is the primary culture hero, creator figure, and trickster of Blackfoot mythology. Created by Apistotoke as the first man and demigod,
source: Wikipedia / Grinnell / Maclean 1893

name: Kipitaakii
description: Kipitaakii (Old Lady) is the wife of Na'pi and a powerful figure in Blackfoot mythology. She was created alongside Na'pi by Apistotoke and assisted him in shaping the world and creating humans. In the pivotal story of death's origin, Na'pi threw a piece of wood into a river saying if it floated people would die and return after four days; if it sank, death would be permanent. The wood floated, but Kipitaakii rejected this outcome and threw a stone instead, which sank. Na'pi thus decreed permanent death. This story establishes her as the one who determined the final nature of human mortality.
appearance: An elderly woman with kind, wise eyes and silver-streaked black hair worn in traditional Blackfoot style. She is often depicted wearing a decorated elk-tooth dress and a blanket for warmth, sitting by a fire where she tells stories to the younger generation.
behavior: The female aspect of creation in Blackfoot tradition, also called Old Woman. She helps Napi in creating the world and often corrects his mistakes. She represents the nurturing, stabilizing feminine force that balances Napi's chaotic creative energy.
habitat: The Blackfoot territory, alongside Na'pi in the creation narrative
cultural_significance: Demonstrates that female figures held significant creative and decision-making power in Blackfoot cosmology. Her choice shaped the fundamental nature of human existence.
summary: Wife of Na'pi and co-creator who determined the permanence of death in Blackfoot mythology
fun_fact: Kipitaakii overruled Na'pi's decision about death by throwing a stone instead of wood into the river, decreeing permanent death for humanity

source: Wikipedia / Maclean 1893

name: Naato'si
description: Naato'si (Natosi) is the Sun god of the Blackfoot people, created by Apistotoke to provide light and warmth to all creation. Alongside his wife Ko'komiki'somm (the Moon), he rules the sky. Naato'si is personified and sometimes identified with the mystical figure of Na'pi (Old Man). By some accounts, Naato'si is equated with the Creator Apistotoke himself. He is a powerful being to whom prayers and offerings are made. His children include the stars and the hero figure Aapisowaahs (Morning Star).
appearance: The Sun in Blackfoot tradition, depicted as a powerful being radiating brilliant golden light. He travels across the sky each day in a journey that brings life to the world. His face is too bright to look upon directly, and his warmth is essential for all creation.
behavior: The ruler of the day who provides light, warmth, and life to all beings. He is married to Ko'komiki'somm the Moon and is a central deity in Blackfoot cosmology. Prayers are offered to him for health, good fortune, and successful hunts.
cultural_significance: A major deity in Blackfoot religion, representing the life-giving power of the sun. Some traditions equate Naato'si with the Creator himself.
summary: Sun god of the Blackfoot people, source of light and warmth
fun_fact: Naato'si's wife is Ko'komiki'somm the Moon, and their children are the stars including Aapisowaahs the Morning Star
seo_description: Naato'si (Natosi) is the Sun god of the Blackfoot people, created by Apistotoke to provide light and warmth to all creation. Alongside his wife Ko'kom
source: Wikipedia / Blackfoot Crossing Historical Park

name: Ko'komiki'somm
description: Ko'komiki'somm (Kokimmikisoom) is the Moon goddess of the Blackfoot people, wife of Naato'si (the Sun). Created by Apistotoke to light the night sky alongside her children the stars. She represents the feminine celestial principle and governs the night. The Moon is associated with cycles, women's mysteries, and the passage of time. Along with Naato'si and the stars, she belongs to the Sky Beings (Sspommitapiiksi) created at the beginning of time.
appearance: The Moon in Blackfoot tradition, personified as a gentle, beautiful woman with silver-white hair and skin that glows with soft lunar light. She wears a robe of midnight blue embroidered with the stars, her children. Her face is serene and nurturing.
behavior: Governs the night, lighting the darkness for all creation. She is the mother of the stars, including the Morning Star Aapisowaahs. She represents the feminine principle of gentleness, constancy, and the quiet power of the night. She watches over lovers and those who travel by night.
weaknesses: wanes and waxes, sometimes absent from the sky
cultural_significance: Represents the feminine divine principle in Blackfoot cosmology and the balance of day and night.
summary: Moon goddess of the Blackfoot people, wife of the Sun and mother of the stars
fun_fact: Ko'komiki'somm's children include all the stars of the night sky, with the Morning Star Aapisowaahs as the most notable
seo_description: Ko'komiki'somm (Kokimmikisoom) is the Moon goddess of the Blackfoot people, wife of Naato'si (the Sun). Created by Apistotoke to light the night sky a
source: Wikipedia / Blackfoot mythology

name: Beaver Spirit
description: The Beaver Spirit is a powerful animal spirit in Blackfoot religion, central to the sacred Beaver Bundle—the most important medicine bundle of the Blackfoot people. According to legend, a Blackfoot man encountered beavers who taught him sacred songs, rituals, and the use of medicinal plants. The Beaver Bundle contains animal skins, pipes, and herbs, each with specific powers. The Beaver Bundle ceremony involves elaborate rituals, singing, and smoking the pipe, used for healing, good fortune, and maintaining balance between human and spirit worlds.
appearance: A giant beaver of supernatural size with glossy brown fur, a broad flat tail that can create river valleys when it strikes the ground, and teeth that can carve through solid rock. In spirit form, it appears as a being of earth and water with powerful, stocky build.
behavior: A powerful water spirit who taught the Blackfoot people how to build lodges, create dams, and manage waterways. He is associated with engineering and construction wisdom. He can cause floods when angered but brings prosperity when respected. He is a symbol of industriousness and family devotion.
habitat: Underwater lodges, rivers, streams, and lakes of Blackfoot territory
weaknesses: requires proper respect and ritual observance
cultural_significance: The Beaver Bundle is the most sacred medicine bundle of the Blackfoot, central to healing and ceremony.
summary: Sacred beaver spirit who taught the Blackfoot the Beaver Bundle ceremony
fun_fact: The Beaver Bundle ceremony is the most sacred and elaborate of all Blackfoot medicine ceremonies, used for healing and maintaining cosmic balance
seo_description: The Beaver Spirit is a powerful animal spirit in Blackfoot religion, central to the sacred Beaver Bundle—the most important medicine bundle of the Bla
source: Wissler / Blackfoot ethnography

name: Pipe Spirit
description: The Pipe Spirit is a sacred spirit in Blackfoot religion that gave the people the Medicine Pipe and taught the associated ceremonies. In Blackfoot tradition, a beautiful woman appeared to a man on a vision quest, giving him a pipe decorated with eagle feathers and teaching the prayers and songs. Alternatively, the Thunder spirit gave the pipe where lightning had struck a tree. The pipe serves as a mediator between the people and the spirit world, used for healing, peace-making, and communicating with Apistotoke. Its keeper must follow strict taboos and conduct annual renewal ceremonies.
appearance: May appear as a beautiful woman bringing the sacred pipe to humanity, or as a Thunder spirit bestowing it from the sky. The pipe itself is a sacred object decorated with eagle feathers, wrapped in sweetgrass, and radiates divine power.
behavior: Mediates between humans and the divine, teaching pipe ceremonies, sacred prayers, and ceremonial songs. Requires strict ritual observance and taboos from its keeper. The Pipe Spirit's ceremonies are central to Blackfoot spiritual life, connecting the people with the Thunder and the Sun.
habitat: Sacred sites, vision quest locations, Medicine Pipe lodges
weaknesses: requires strict taboos and proper ritual observance
cultural_significance: The Medicine Pipe society is one of the most important spiritual societies of the Blackfoot people.
summary: Sacred spirit who gave the Blackfoot the Medicine Pipe and its ceremonies
fun_fact: The Medicine Pipe was found where lightning had struck a tree, and the Pipe Spirit instructed the finder to form a society of pipe keepers

source: Grinnell / Blackfoot oral tradition

name: Thunder Spirit
description: The Thunder Spirit is a powerful sky spirit in Blackfoot mythology, associated with storms, thunder, and lightning. According to legend, the Thunder spirit gave the Blackfoot the sacred pipe, where lightning had struck a tree and left a beautifully carved pipe. The Thunder spirit instructed the finder to form a society of pipe keepers and taught the songs and rituals for its use. Thunder is associated with the renewal of life in spring and is both feared and respected for its power to bring life-giving rain or destructive storms.
appearance: A powerful sky being with a voice of thunder and eyes that flash lightning, often depicted as a great bird or a massive humanoid wrapped in storm clouds. Its wings darken the sky, and its breath stirs the winds across the plains.
behavior: Controls thunder, lightning, and storms. It is both feared and respected, bringing the rains that sustain life but also destructive storms. It must be honored with proper ceremonies and is associated with the Medicine Pipe tradition.
habitat: The sky, storm clouds, lightning-struck places
cultural_significance: The Thunder spirit is associated with the origin of the Medicine Pipe, one of the most sacred objects of the Blackfoot people.
summary: Blackfoot storm spirit associated with thunder, lightning, and the origin of the sacred pipe
fun_fact: The Blackfoot believe the first Medicine Pipe was found where lightning struck a tree, and the Thunder spirit taught the songs and rituals for its use
seo_description: The Thunder Spirit is a powerful sky spirit in Blackfoot mythology, associated with storms, thunder, and lightning. According to legend, the Thunder s
source: Blackfoot oral tradition

name: Star Spirit
description: Star Spirit appears in Arapaho folklore as a celestial being who can take human form. In the Star Husband story, two Arapaho women lay outside their tipi and one wished to marry a star. The next day, a handsome young man appeared—the star in human form, come to claim his bride. She went with him to the sky world, but grew homesick. Told she could return if she did not eat certain food, she broke the taboo and found herself back on Earth. Her star husband appeared no more, but she gave birth to a son who became a legendary Arapaho hero. Star spirits represent the connection between humans and the celestial realm.
appearance: A brilliant point of light in the night sky, too bright to look at directly. In human form, the Star Spirit appears as a luminous being wrapped in a cloak of starry light, its face too radiant to make out clearly, surrounded by a corona of celestial fire.
behavior: A celestial being that carries prayers from the earth to the Creator. Stars are considered the spirits of the departed who watch over their living relatives. The Star Spirit guides travelers, marks the seasons, and holds the stories of the people written in the sky.
habitat: The night sky, the celestial realm
weaknesses: may be bound by celestial taboos
cultural_significance: Stars are the children of the Sun and Moon in Blackfoot cosmology, representing the connection between the earthly and celestial worlds.
summary: Arapaho star being who married an earthly woman and fathered a legendary hero
fun_fact: An Arapaho woman who married a Star Spirit gave birth to a son who became a legendary hero; the star husband disappeared when she broke a food taboo
seo_description: Star Spirit appears in Arapaho folklore as a celestial being who can take human form. In the Star Husband story, two Arapaho women lay outside their t
source: Blackfoot folklore / Grinnell

name: Sweet Medicine
description: Sweet Medicine (Motsé'eóeve) is the greatest prophet and law-giver of the Cheyenne people. He journeyed to Nóávóse (Bear Butte) in the Black Hills where Ma'heo'o gave him the four sacred arrows (Maahótse)—two for hunting success and two for warfare. He received the structure of Cheyenne government (Council of Forty-Four), the military societies, the legal system, and the Sun Dance ceremony. Beginning as a troublesome trickster figure, he transformed into a wise lawgiver. He invented the hoop-and-stick game (chunkey) and predicted the coming of horses, white men, and the loss of the buffalo.
appearance: A great Cheyenne prophet and culture hero depicted as a wise man with a gentle face, wearing traditional Cheyenne clothing adorned with sacred medicine bundles. His eyes carry the knowledge of the Cheyenne people, and his hands hold the sacred laws.
behavior: A divine messenger who brought the Cheyenne people their sacred ceremonies, laws, and moral code. He taught the Sacred Arrow ceremony and the Sun Dance. He established the principles of tribal governance and the proper way to live in harmony with the Great Spirit.
habitat: Bear Butte (Nóávóse) in the Black Hills, the Cheyenne territory
weaknesses: chose the spirit of old age and death at Bear Butte
cultural_significance: The foundational culture hero of the Cheyenne, comparable to Moses in Judeo-Christian tradition. His four sacred arrows remain the most sacred Cheyenne objects.
summary: Great prophet and law-giver of the Cheyenne who received the four sacred arrows
fun_fact: Sweet Medicine was offered a choice among spirit guides at Bear Butte and chose one dressed in yellow—symbolizing old age and death—sealing humanity's fate to grow old and die
seo_description: Sweet Medicine (Motsé'eóeve) is the greatest prophet and law-giver of the Cheyenne people. He journeyed to Nóávóse (Bear Butte) in the Black Hills whe
source: World History Encyclopedia / Wikipedia / Cheyenne oral tradition

name: Ma'heo'o
description: Ma'heo'o (also Maheo, Heammawihio) is the Creator and supreme being in Cheyenne religion, meaning 'sacred power' or 'Great Mystery.' Also known as Heammawihio ('Spider Above'), Ma'heo'o is a divine spirit without human form or attributes. According to Cheyenne creation, Ma'heo'o existed before all things and created the world from mud brought by a waterbird (coot), then formed the earth on a turtle's back. He created plants, animals, and humans, and gave the sacred ceremonies through Sweet Medicine and Erect Horns. He is rarely personified in folklore and represents the ultimate sacred power.
appearance: No physical form, being a divine sacred power beyond human comprehension. Sometimes referred to as Spider Above (Heammawihio), emphasizing creative intelligence rather than a literal spider form. He is the invisible weaver of the universe's fabric.
behavior: Creator of the universe who receives prayers through the sacred pipe. He delegated the teaching of humans to culture heroes Sweet Medicine and Erect Horns. He is the source of all sacred power and the ultimate authority in Cheyenne cosmology.
habitat: The heavens, above all creation (Heammawihio = 'Spider Above')
cultural_significance: The supreme being of the Cheyenne, representing sacred power and ultimate creative authority.
summary: Creator god and supreme being of the Cheyenne people
fun_fact: Despite missionary claims, Ma'heo'o does NOT mean 'All-Father' in Cheyenne—the word's literal meaning is simply 'sacred power' or 'Great Mystery.'
seo_description: Ma'heo'o (also Maheo, Heammawihio) is the Creator and supreme being in Cheyenne religion, meaning 'sacred power' or 'Great Mystery.' Also known as Hea
source: Native-Languages.org / Cheyenne oral tradition

name: Erect Horns
description: Erect Horns (Tomȯsévėséhe) was the prophet of the Só'taeo'o people who later merged with the Cheyenne. He received the Ésevone (Sacred Buffalo Hat) at Tȯhóonévose (Stone Hammer Mountain) near the Great Lakes. The sacred hat represents female power, complementing the male power of the Sacred Arrows—together they form the two great covenants of the Cheyenne Nation. Erect Horns gave the people the Sun Dance ceremony and convinced the tribe to abandon their sedentary agricultural lifestyle, adopt the nomadic Plains horse culture, and rely on buffalo for survival.
appearance: A powerful Cheyenne culture hero depicted as a warrior wearing a headdress with horns that symbolize his spiritual authority and connection to the Buffalo. His face is strong and determined, marked by the wisdom gained from his spiritual journeys.
behavior: A prophet who brought the Cheyenne the Sacred Hat (Mutsihi) ceremonies and taught them how to live rightly. He established important spiritual traditions including proper marriage customs and the laws governing warfare.
habitat: Stone Hammer Mountain (Minnesota/Great Lakes region), later the Plains
cultural_significance: Erect Horns' vision transformed the Cheyenne way of life, and the Sacred Buffalo Hat remains one of the two most sacred Cheyenne objects.
summary: Prophet who brought the Sacred Buffalo Hat and transformed Cheyenne society
fun_fact: Erect Horns convinced the Cheyenne ancestors to abandon earth-lodge agriculture and adopt the nomadic Plains buffalo-hunting lifestyle, fundamentally changing their culture
seo_description: Erect Horns (Tomȯsévėséhe) was the prophet of the Só'taeo'o people who later merged with the Cheyenne. He received the Ésevone (Sacred Buffalo Hat) at
source: Wikipedia / Cheyenne oral tradition

name: Wihio
description: Wihio (Ve'ho'e) is the Cheyenne trickster figure, a spider-like being whose name means 'spider' and is related to the word for 'chief' and the Creator's name Heammawihio. He appears as a man in most tales, both clever and foolish, wise and ridiculous. His stories range from silly antics (losing his eyeballs, falling for obvious tricks) to important cultural tales (releasing the buffalo from the wonderful sack). Wihio teaches Cheyenne values through humor—greed, selfishness, and foolishness always lead to his comeuppance while cleverness and generosity triumph. The name eventually came to mean 'white man' after European contact.
appearance: A wiry, clever-looking Cheyenne man with a sly grin and quick, darting eyes that are always looking for an opportunity. He wears simple buckskin clothing and moves with an energetic, restless quality that suggests he is always up to something.
behavior: The Cheyenne trickster figure who creates mischief and teaches lessons through his foolish behavior. He is always looking for an easy meal or a way to avoid work. His schemes often backfire spectacularly, and his adventures serve as teaching stories about greed and dishonesty.
habitat: The Cheyenne territory, the plains, wherever people are gathering
weaknesses: greed, pride, and foolishness cause his downfalls
cultural_significance: Wihio's stories are among the most popular Cheyenne tales, teaching cultural values through humor and cautionary examples.
summary: Spider trickster figure of the Cheyenne people who teaches through foolish adventures
fun_fact: The Cheyenne word for white man (ve'ho'e) comes from Wihio's name—the Cheyenne named white people after the trickster, not vice versa
seo_description: Wihio (Ve'ho'e) is the Cheyenne trickster figure, a spider-like being whose name means 'spider' and is related to the word for 'chief' and the Creator
source: Wihio Tales / World History Encyclopedia / Native-Languages.org

name: Nonoma
description: Nonoma is the Cheyenne spirit of thunder, a powerful being who controls storms and brings rain to the plains. When Nonoma flaps his wings, thunder rolls across the sky. He is both feared and respected—his storms can bring life-giving rain for crops and buffalo or destructive hail and lightning. The Cheyenne perform ceremonies to honor Nonoma and ask for his blessing. The first thunder of spring signals the time for planting and the Sun Dance ceremony. Nonoma represents the powerful, renewing force of storms that brings life to the plains.
appearance: A majestic white buffalo cow with a luminous, pure-white coat that seems to glow with an inner light. Her eyes are calm and wise, and she moves with a grace that commands reverence. She is surrounded by an aura of sacred power.
behavior: The sacred white buffalo of the Cheyenne, considered the most powerful of all buffalo spirits. Her appearance is a powerful omen of significant change or spiritual renewal. She is deeply honored and her rare appearances are celebrated as sacred events.
habitat: The sky, storm clouds, the western horizon
weaknesses: can be propitiated with proper ceremony
cultural_significance: Nonoma's spring thunder signals the time for planting and the Sun Dance, connecting the spirit to Cheyenne agricultural and ceremonial cycles.
summary: Cheyenne thunder spirit who controls storms and brings life-giving rain
fun_fact: The first thunder of spring announced by Nonoma signals the proper time for the Cheyenne Sun Dance ceremony and planting season
seo_description: Nonoma is the Cheyenne spirit of thunder, a powerful being who controls storms and brings rain to the plains. When Nonoma flaps his wings, thunder rol
source: Cheyenne folklore

name: Old Woman's Water
description: Old Woman's Water is a powerful water spirit in Cheyenne mythology, associated with a sacred healing spring. An old woman who lived by a sacred spring found that her water had healing powers. She shared it with a young wounded warrior who was miraculously healed. The woman then revealed herself as a manifestation of the earth's power. She gave the warrior a buffalo cap made from the scalp of a sacred buffalo, which became the Ésevone (Sacred Buffalo Hat) that could summon buffalo herds and protect the people. She taught the rituals needed to care for the cap and warned that neglect would cause the buffalo to disappear.
appearance: A kind-faced old Cheyenne woman with long silver hair and gentle, knowing eyes. She carries a water gourd that never empties, and her presence brings a feeling of peace and maternal comfort. She wears simple clothing adorned with medicinal herbs.
behavior: A protective female spirit associated with healing waters and purification. She provides water to the thirsty and heals the sick with sacred water. She is particularly associated with the health and well-being of women and children in Cheyenne tradition.
habitat: Sacred springs, specifically the spring associated with the Buffalo Hat origin
weaknesses: requirements for proper ritual care of sacred objects
cultural_significance: Associated with the origin of the Ésevone (Sacred Buffalo Hat), one of the two most sacred Cheyenne ceremonial objects.
summary: Cheyenne water spirit who bestowed the Sacred Buffalo Hat through her healing spring
fun_fact: Old Woman's Water gave the sacred buffalo cap that became the Ésevone—the female counterpart to the male Sacred Arrows of the Cheyenne
seo_description: Old Woman's Water is a powerful water spirit in Cheyenne mythology, associated with a sacred healing spring. An old woman who lived by a sacred spring
source: Grinnell / Cheyenne oral tradition

name: Ésevone
description: Ésevone is the Sacred Buffalo Hat of the Cheyenne people, one of the two most sacred ceremonial objects of the Cheyenne Nation (alongside the Maahótse Sacred Arrows). Made from the skin of a buffalo cow's head, ornamented with a pair of buffalo horns that have been shaved down, flattened, and decorated. Ésevone represents female power, while the Sacred Arrows represent male power. It was brought to the people by the prophet Erect Horns (or Standing-on-the-Ground). The hat could summon buffalo herds and protect the people. Its keeper must follow strict taboos and perform annual renewal ceremonies.
appearance: The Sacred Buffalo Hat, personified as a powerful spirit wearing a buffalo-horn headdress, its eyes holding the ancient wisdom of the Cheyenne people. The hat itself is made from the hide of a sacred buffalo and adorned with sweetgrass and eagle feathers.
behavior: A sacred tribal object and the spirit it embodies, representing the spiritual and political unity of the Cheyenne nation. The Sacred Hat ceremonies ensure the well-being of the people and are among the most important religious observances in Cheyenne tradition.
habitat: Kept in a sacred bundle, cared for by designated keepers within the Cheyenne nation
weaknesses: neglect of proper ceremony causes its power to wane
cultural_significance: Together with the Sacred Arrows, Ésevone forms the two great covenants of the Cheyenne Nation, central to Cheyenne religious identity.
summary: Sacred Buffalo Hat of the Cheyenne, representing female spiritual power
fun_fact: When the Buffalo Hat was neglected by its keepers, the Cheyenne believe spiritual protection weakened, contributing to later misfortunes
seo_description: Ésevone is the Sacred Buffalo Hat of the Cheyenne people, one of the two most sacred ceremonial objects of the Cheyenne Nation (alongside the Maahótse
source: Cheyenne oral tradition / Grinnell / Powell

name: Great Spirit
description: The Great Spirit is the supreme creator and sustaining power in Comanche religion. According to Comanche creation, the Great Spirit collected swirls of dust from the four directions—north, south, east, and west—and molded them into strong, powerful figures, breathing life into them to create the Comanche people. The Great Spirit cast a shape-shifting demon into a bottomless pit for tormenting the people, but the demon shattered into pieces that became rattlesnakes, scorpions, and spiders. The Great Spirit also caused healing springs to bubble up after battles and provides guidance through visions and dreams.
appearance: No specific physical form, being a supreme spiritual power beyond mortal comprehension. As the creative force behind the universe, the Great Spirit is present in the wind, the elements, and all of creation, felt rather than seen.
behavior: Creator and sustainer of the Comanche people, protecting them from evil forces. Provides healing, guidance, and maintains cosmic order. The Great Spirit is the source of all life and the ultimate power to whom all prayers are directed.
habitat: The heavens, the spirit world, omnipresent
cultural_significance: Central figure in Comanche religion, representing the ultimate source of life, protection, and spiritual authority.
summary: Supreme creator god of the Comanche people
fun_fact: In Comanche creation, the Great Spirit molded the first people from dust gathered from the four directions, giving them the strength of storms and wind
seo_description: The Great Spirit is the supreme creator and sustaining power in Comanche religion. According to Comanche creation, the Great Spirit collected swirls o
source: Ya-Native Network / The Singing Scoutmaster

name: Shape-shifting Demon
description: The Shape-shifting Demon is a malevolent entity in Comanche creation mythology. It formed in the shadows, envious of the powerful Comanche people created by the Great Spirit. It tormented the Comanche by taking many forms. The Great Spirit cast the demon into a bottomless pit, but before falling, the demon shattered into countless pieces that took refuge in the fangs and stingers of rattlesnakes, scorpions, and spiders, continuing to harm people to this day. This explains the origin of venomous creatures and the existence of evil in the world.
appearance: A terrifying entity that can assume any form, most commonly appearing as a grotesque animal-human hybrid with glowing eyes, sharp claws, and a twisted, nightmarish shape that changes constantly, making it impossible to describe consistently.
behavior: A malevolent being that stalks the night, appearing to those who break tribal laws or wander alone after dark. It uses its shapeshifting ability to trick and terrify its victims. It is a warning figure used to enforce moral behavior in Comanche tradition.
habitat: Shadows, bottomless pit (after being cast out by the Great Spirit); snip its pieces inhabit venomous creatures
weaknesses: could not withstand the Great Spirit's power
cultural_significance: Explains the origin of venomous creatures and the presence of evil in the world from a Comanche perspective.
summary: Evil shape-shifting entity from Comanche creation mythology
fun_fact: Before falling into the bottomless pit, the shape-shifting demon shattered into pieces that became rattlesnakes, scorpions, and spiders
seo_description: The Shape-shifting Demon is a malevolent entity in Comanche creation mythology. It formed in the shadows, envious of the powerful Comanche people crea
source: Ya-Native Network / Comanche oral tradition

name: Wolf Spirit
description: The Wolf Spirit is a powerful animal spirit and guardian figure in Comanche mythology. In the story How the Buffalo Were Released, a Wolf spirit guided a young Comanche warrior to the cave where buffalo were hidden, transformed him into a buffalo calf to infiltrate the herd, and taught the people how to hunt the buffalo with respect. In vision quest stories, Wolf appears as a spirit guide granting strength, courage, and tracking ability to warriors who fast and seek visions. Wolf is considered a brother and protector to the Comanche people.
appearance: A magnificent wolf of supernatural size with silver-gray fur that seems to shimmer in the moonlight, intelligent golden eyes that reflect ancient wisdom, and a presence that commands respect from all creatures of the plains.
behavior: A powerful guide and protector who teaches hunting skills, pack loyalty, and survival wisdom. The Wolf Spirit is associated with courage, family bonds, and the ability to navigate both the physical and spiritual worlds. He is a revered teacher in Comanche tradition.
habitat: The plains, mountains, vision quest sites
weaknesses: requires those he helps to never kill wolves
cultural_significance: Wolf is one of the most important animal spirit guides in Comanche tradition, associated with warrior strength and hunting prowess.
summary: Comanche wolf spirit guide who grants strength, courage, and hunting ability
fun_fact: In Comanche tradition, Wolf appears to warriors on vision quests and grants power in exchange for a promise to never kill wolves

source: MythBeasts / Comanche oral tradition

name: Wind Spirit
description: The Wind Spirit is an elemental force in Comanche mythology. In the creation story, the Great Spirit infused the first people with the spirit of the wind, giving them strength of mighty storms. In the Release of the Wild Animals, a Wind spirit helped a brave warrior open the underground cavern where wild animals were confined, unleashing deer, antelope, elk, bears, wolves, and mountain lions across the plains. The Wind spirit represents freedom, power, and the unseen forces that shape the world. Wind carries prayers and is a messenger between worlds.
appearance: An invisible but powerful presence felt as moving air, manifesting as swirling dust devils, rustling grass, and bending trees. When visible, the Wind Spirit appears as a swirling, translucent form that shifts and flows like the air itself.
behavior: Controls the winds that bring weather, carry messages, and shape the landscape. The Wind Spirit brings the rains, drives away the heat, and carries prayers to the Great Spirit. It has moods ranging from gentle breezes to destructive tornadoes.
habitat: The sky, the plains, the four directions
cultural_significance: Wind is one of the fundamental elements in Comanche cosmology, carrying prayers and connecting the earthly and spiritual realms.
summary: Comanche wind spirit that aids humans and carries prayers to the spirit world
fun_fact: In Comanche belief, the wind spirit helped release wild animals from an underground cavern where a protective spirit had confined them

source: Comanche folklore / Native Languages

name: Antelope Spirit
description: The Antelope Spirit is a messenger and omen spirit in Comanche mythology. In the story of Hotuiyi, a Comanche hunting party pursuing antelope encountered a strange antelope with glowing eyes—a spirit messenger. The antelope led the hunters to a hidden spring and traced a path around a canyon where enemies lay in ambush, saving them from both thirst and attack. Thereafter, the Comanche considered antelope sightings as omens: if the antelope runs east, good fortune follows; if west, danger approaches.
appearance: A beautiful antelope with a radiant, glowing coat and luminous eyes that seem to hold the light of distant stars. Its horns are tipped with light, and it moves with an ethereal grace, leaving faint traces of light in its path across the plains.
behavior: A messenger and guide that warns of danger and leads lost travelers to water. Provides omens through directional movement. If an antelope runs east in Comanche tradition, it signals good fortune; if west, danger approaches. It serves as a spiritual guide between worlds.
habitat: The plains, particularly around canyons and water sources
cultural_significance: Antelope sightings are interpreted as omens in Comanche tradition, with directional movement carrying specific meanings.
summary: Comanche antelope spirit that serves as a messenger and omen giver
fun_fact: If an antelope runs east in Comanche tradition, it signals good fortune; if west, danger approaches

source: Comanche folklore

name: Skunk
description: Skunk appears in Comanche trickster tales as a clever animal who often outwits Coyote. In the famous story Skunk Outwits Coyote, Skunk finds Coyote trying to catch prairie dogs by blocking their holes and waiting with his mouth open. Skunk offers to help, then instead of driving prairie dogs toward Coyote, walks up and sprays him in the face. Coyote runs away howling, and the prairie dogs escape. Skunk proves that even the cleverest schemer can be outsmarted, and that brute force does not always prevail.
appearance: A black-and-white skunk of unusually large size, with an impressive bushy tail that it carries high as a warning. Its markings are stark and distinctive, and its presence is unmistakable. Despite its small size, it commands respect from all creatures.
behavior: A trickster figure who teaches about respect and the power of being underestimated. The skunk's powerful defense represents the idea that size and strength are not the only forms of power. It is respected for its confidence and its ability to defend itself against much larger foes.
habitat: The plains and prairies of Comanche territory
weaknesses: small size, relies on trickery rather than strength
cultural_significance: Skunk stories teach Comanche values about cleverness overcoming brute force.
summary: Clever trickster animal in Comanche folklore
fun_fact: In Comanche tales, Skunk uses its signature spray to outwit the much larger and supposedly smarter Coyote

source: Native Languages of the Americas

name: Old Man Coyote
description: Old Man Coyote (Isáahkawuattee, Akbaatatdia) is the central creator and trickster figure of Crow mythology. He was alone upon a great ocean when he saw two male ducks and asked them to dive for mud, which he used to build an island that grew into all the lands of Earth. He shaped mountains, rivers, and valleys, then molded humans from clay and created women so they would be happy. Old Man Coyote is simultaneously the world's creator and its most unreliable inhabitant—enormously clever yet occasionally foolish, both source of everything and an ongoing embarrassment. He is still in the world, still making things and making mistakes.
appearance: An old man who shifts easily into a coyote form, with sharp, knowing eyes and a sly grin. In human form he appears as a weathered elder with gray hair and a hunched posture, but his eyes betray the clever coyote spirit within.
behavior: The Crow trickster and transformer who shaped the world through his adventures. He stole fire for humanity, created the landscape, and taught essential skills. However, his greed and arrogance often led to trouble. He represents both the creative and destructive powers of the trickster.
habitat: The Crow territory (Montana, Wyoming), the plains, all of creation
weaknesses: pride and foolishness cause his endless troubles
cultural_significance: Central figure of Crow religion, embodying the paradox of a Creator who is both wise and foolish, sacred and ridiculous.
summary: Creator god and trickster of Crow mythology who made the world from mud brought by a duck
fun_fact: Old Man Coyote is still active in the world—the Crow relationship with him is not of creature to Creator but of a people to a very old relative who is the source of everything and an ongoing embarrassment
seo_description: Old Man Coyote (Isáahkawuattee, Akbaatatdia) is the central creator and trickster figure of Crow mythology. He was alone upon a great ocean when he sa
source: Wikipedia / Crow religion / Native-Languages.org

name: Bones Together
description: Bones Together is a fearsome monster in Crow mythology, a skeletal being with impenetrable bone armor. Seven Bison and their human companion fought against Bones Together when the monster threatened them. Each bison charged but broke their legs against Bones Together's bony hide. Finally the human companion, blessed by an eagle with the power to transform into a feather, faced the monster. Bones Together charged four times, but the man turned into a feather and wafted out of harm's way. On the fourth charge, the man shot an arrow into Bones Together's rectum, piercing his heart and killing the monster.
appearance: A monstrous giant covered entirely in impenetrable bone armor, with bones protruding from its body in terrifying patterns. Its face is a skull-like mask of fused bone, and its hands end in bony claws. It towers over the landscape like a walking skeleton.
behavior: A fearsome monster that terrorized the Crow people, demanding tribute and devouring anyone who crossed its path. It was so heavily armored that weapons shattered against its bone plating. The Seven Bison heroically fought it and ultimately the Sweat Lodge ceremony was needed to heal them.
weaknesses: the arrow to his rectum—the one unarmored spot
cultural_significance: His defeat led to the first Sweat Lodge ceremony and the creation of the Big Dipper from the Seven Bison.
summary: Bone-armored monster from Crow mythology defeated in the first Sweat Lodge story
fun_fact: Bones Together could only be killed by shooting an arrow into his rectum, the one spot not protected by bone armor

source: Wikipedia / Yellowtail 1991

name: Seven Bison
description: Seven Bison are sacred spirit animals in Crow mythology who fought against the monster Bones Together. After breaking their legs against Bones Together's impenetrable bone armor, they were healed through the first Sweat Lodge ceremony performed by their human companion. After this victory and healing, the Creator raised the Seven Bison into the sky to become the Big Dipper constellation, where they can be seen eternally following the seasons. They represent sacrifice, healing, and the celestial connection between earth and sky.
appearance: Seven powerful bison with massive dark coats, curved horns, and eyes that burn with the fire of courage. After their apotheosis, they appear as seven brilliant stars in the night sky, forming the Big Dipper constellation that guides travelers.
behavior: Courageous warrior spirits who fought against the monster Bones Together, breaking their legs against its impenetrable bone armor. They were healed through the first Sweat Lodge ceremony and then ascended to the sky as stars, becoming the Big Dipper.
habitat: Originally the plains, later the night sky as the Big Dipper
weaknesses: broke their legs against Bones Together's armor
cultural_significance: The Seven Bison's transformation into the Big Dipper connects Crow cosmology to the night sky.
summary: Seven sacred bison who became the Big Dipper in Crow mythology
fun_fact: After being healed by the first Sweat Lodge ceremony, the Seven Bison rose into the sky to become the Big Dipper constellation
seo_description: Seven Bison are sacred spirit animals in Crow mythology who fought against the monster Bones Together. After breaking their legs against Bones Togethe
source: Yellowtail 1991 / Crow tradition

name: Eagle Spirit
description: Eagle Spirit is a powerful guardian and teacher in Crow mythology. In the Bones Together story, the Eagle blessed the human companion with the power to transform into a feather, which allowed him to evade the monster's charges and defeat Bones Together. Eagles are considered sacred birds in Crow culture, associated with the sky, the sun, and divine power. Eagle feathers are used in ceremonies and headdresses as symbols of spiritual authority. Eagle Spirit guides warriors and vision seekers, granting them the power of keen sight and spiritual elevation.
appearance: A majestic golden eagle of enormous size with wings that span the horizon, feathers of burnished gold, and eyes like drops of the sun. When it descends, the wind itself seems to pause in reverence. It is the most revered of all winged creatures in Crow tradition.
behavior: The most powerful of the winged spirits, serving as a messenger between humans and the Creator. Eagle feathers are the highest honor a Crow warrior can receive. The Eagle Spirit represents courage, vision, spiritual power, and the ability to soar above earthly concerns.
habitat: The sky, high mountains, sacred sites
cultural_significance: Eagle feathers are among the most sacred objects in Crow and Plains Indian culture, representing spiritual authority and connection to the divine.
summary: Crow eagle spirit that grants transformation powers and spiritual vision
fun_fact: The Eagle Spirit blessed a Crow warrior with the power to become a feather, allowing him to defeat the invulnerable Bones Together

source: Yellowtail 1991 / Crow tradition

name: Mannegishi
description: The Mannegishi (also known as Awwakkule, Nirumbee) are the Little People of Crow and Cree folklore—small, bald humanoid beings with large bulging eyes and tiny tan bodies. They are tricksters who live in rocky areas, along riverbanks, and especially in the Pryor Mountains of Montana. These beings are known for playing pranks, stealing objects, and sometimes more malevolent acts like stealing children. Despite their troublesome nature, they can also confer spiritual blessings (maxpe) to those who seek them through fasting. They are incredibly strong for their size—legends say a Mannegishi can kill and carry off a full-grown bull elk.
appearance: A small, child-like creature with smooth gray skin, large dark eyes, and a thin, frail body. It has long fingers and toes for gripping rocks, and it moves with surprising speed through the canyons and badlands. Its head is slightly oversized, giving it a distinctive silhouette against the sky.
behavior: Lives in rock crevices and canyon walls, emerging at twilight. It is shy and avoids human contact, though it is curious about human activities. It is known to play tricks on travelers by throwing pebbles or making strange sounds echo through the canyons. It represents the mysterious spirits of the rocky landscape.
habitat: Rocky areas, riverbanks, the Pryor Mountains of Montana, Medicine Rocks
weaknesses: can be appeased with offerings of arrows, cloth, or tobacco
cultural_significance: The Pryor Mountains are sacred to the Crow because the Little People live there. The Crow refused to enter certain areas without leaving offerings.
summary: Little People tricksters of Crow folklore who live in the Pryor Mountains

name: Chief No Vitals
description: Chief No Vitals (also known as No Vitals) is a Crow culture hero who discovered tobacco and established the Tobacco Society (Bacu'sua). According to tradition, he was instructed by the Creator Akbaatatdia to seek the sacred plant at Devils Lake in eastern North Dakota. The Creator told him that the worship of tobacco would help the Crow honor God and maintain their connection to the spirit world. Chief No Vitals found the plant and brought it back, establishing the Tobacco Society to ensure all rites and rituals for cultivating tobacco are performed correctly. Smoking tobacco carries prayers directly to God as smoke ascends to the heavens.
appearance: A tall, gaunt warrior figure with a skeletal appearance, wearing traditional Crow warrior regalia. His body shows no signs of life, yet he moves with purpose. His eyes are hollow and dark, and his presence is accompanied by an eerie stillness that makes the air feel cold.
behavior: A death spirit who leads the souls of the dead to the afterlife. He does not harm the living but his appearance is an omen that someone will soon die. He is a psychopomp, guiding Crow warriors who have fallen in battle to the spirit world where they join their ancestors.
habitat: Devils Lake (eastern North Dakota), the Crow territory
cultural_significance: The Tobacco Society is one of the most important Crow spiritual societies, ensuring the sacred use of tobacco for communication with the Creator.
summary: Crow culture hero who discovered tobacco and founded the Tobacco Society
fun_fact: Chief No Vitals was instructed by the Creator to find tobacco at Devils Lake and establish the Tobacco Society so the Crow could send their prayers to God through smoke

name: Akbaatatdia
description: Akbaatatdia (One Who Has Made Everything), also known as Iichíkbaalee (First Doer) and Isáahkawuattee (Old Man Coyote), is the supreme Creator in Crow religion. This singular omnipotent god created the entire universe. The Crow believe the universe consists of three worlds: the physical world (the smallest), the spirit world (the intermediate realm), and the third world where God alone dwells. Akbaatatdia is omnipresent and omnipotent. Because God created everything, all of nature is sacred, and all religions are considered valid paths to the same Creator.
appearance: The first woman and mother of the Crow people, depicted as a beautiful woman with long black hair, dressed in intricately decorated buckskin. Her face is serene and wise, marked by the depth of her experience as the matriarch of the Crow nation.
behavior: The first woman created by the Creator, who became the mother of the Crow people. She taught women the arts of tanning hides, gathering food, and raising children. She represents the nurturing, life-giving force in Crow cosmology and is honored as the tribal matriarch.
habitat: The third world (beyond the physical and spirit worlds), also omnipresent
cultural_significance: The supreme concept in Crow religion; snip Akbaatatdia created everything and is in contact with the Crow during every aspect of daily life.
summary: Supreme Creator god of the Crow people who made the universe
fun_fact: The Crow believe Akbaatatdia created three worlds: the physical world (smallest), the spirit world, and the third world where God alone dwells
seo_description: Akbaatatdia (One Who Has Made Everything), also known as Iichíkbaalee (First Doer) and Isáahkawuattee (Old Man Coyote), is the supreme Creator in Crow
source: Wikipedia / Frey 1997

name: Aapisowaahs
description: Aapisowaahs (Morning Star) is a celestial hero in Crow mythology, the son of Naato'si the Sun and Ko'komiki'somm the Moon, created by Apistotoke. He lights the night sky as the morning star and is associated with new beginnings, hope, and guidance. In Crow belief, Old Man Coyote traveled to the sky world and brought knowledge of the Morning Star back to the people. The Morning Star is honored at dawn with prayers and songs in Crow ceremonies. Its appearance signals the time for certain rituals and serves as a reminder of the Crow's connection to the celestial realm.
appearance: The Morning Star in Crow tradition, appearing as a brilliant point of light in the eastern sky at dawn. In personified form, Aapisowaahs appears as a young warrior with a radiant aura, his body glowing with the golden light of the approaching dawn.
behavior: Heralds the arrival of the sun each day, marking the boundary between night and day. As the Morning Star, Aapisowaahs is a guide and protector of souls, leading the spirits of the dead on their journey to the afterlife.
habitat: The eastern sky, the celestial realm
cultural_significance: The Morning Star is a significant figure in Crow celestial cosmology, marking time for important ceremonies.
summary: Crow morning star deity, son of the Sun and Moon
fun_fact: Old Man Coyote traveled to the sky world and brought knowledge of Aapisowaahs back to the Crow people

name: Morning Star
description: Morning Star is a powerful male warrior god in Pawnee mythology, the first being created by Tirawa. Placed in the East, he was commanded to overcome the Evening Star in the West, who resisted the divine plan to create humankind. Morning Star fought and conquered forces in the western sky with his fireball to mate with her, producing the first human. He is associated with warfare, sacrifice, and cosmic order. The Skidi Pawnee performed the Morning Star sacrifice ceremony—a ritual sacrifice of a captive girl to ensure agricultural fertility—reenacting the cosmic battle between Morning Star and Evening Star.
appearance: A brilliant warrior spirit appearing as the Morning Star, Opirikuts is depicted as a powerful warrior riding across the dawn sky. His body radiates golden light, and he carries a shining star as his shield. He is the son or messenger of Tirawa.
behavior: A bringer of light and life who battles the forces of darkness. Associated with warfare and leadership, he is the patron of Pawnee warriors. His star governs the timing of important ceremonies, including the Morning Star sacrifice.
habitat: The eastern sky at dawn, the celestial realm
weaknesses: cannot prevent his wife from leaving
cultural_significance: Explains the presence of the Morning Star in the dawn sky and teaches lessons about obedience and the consequences of broken taboos.
summary: Pawnee warrior god who created the first human through cosmic battle with Evening Star
fun_fact: The Skidi Pawnee performed the Morning Star sacrifice ceremony where a captive girl was symbolically transformed into Evening Star and sacrificed to ensure fertility

name: Seven Rams
description: Seven Rams are magnificent spirit animals in Crow mythology. A Crow man of immense ability and power once encountered them in the mountains. Confident in his own strength, he thought he could overpower them. But the Seven Rams taught him humility—despite his great power, the man learned he must respect the Sweat Lodge and its ceremonies, for the lodge's power was greater than any individual's. The Rams demonstrated that true strength comes from spiritual purity and connection to the Creator, not from physical prowess.
appearance: Seven massive bighorn rams with powerful curled horns and thick woolly coats, standing together in perfect formation. Their eyes glow with intelligence and determination, and their hooves strike sparks from the stone as they move across the mountains.
behavior: Brave warrior spirits who fought a great battle to protect the Crow people. After their heroic deeds, they were transformed into a constellation in the night sky. They represent courage, unity, and self-sacrifice for the good of the tribe.
cultural_significance: Teach the importance of humility and submission to spiritual discipline in Crow culture.
summary: Seven spirit rams who taught humility through spiritual power in Crow mythology
fun_fact: The Seven Rams taught a powerful Crow man that Sweat Lodge ceremonial power exceeds any individual strength or ability

source: McClearly 2012 / Crow tradition

name: Tirawa
description: Tirawa (Atíʼas Tirawa, 'Our Father Above') is the supreme creator god of the Pawnee people. He created the universe and placed the Morning Star in the East and the Evening Star in the West. The Morning Star, a male warrior god, was created first. The female Evening Star resisted the divine plan to create humankind, so Morning Star fought and overcame forces in the western sky to mate with her, creating the first human (a girl). Tirawa taught the Pawnee tattooing, fire-building, hunting, agriculture, speech, clothing, religious rituals, and sacrifice. His wife is Atira (Mother Corn), goddess of the Earth.
appearance: The supreme sky god of the Pawnee, depicted as a vast expanse of blue sky that encompasses all things. When manifested, Tirawa appears as an immense, formless presence of pure light and power, containing the sun, moon, and stars within his being.
behavior: Creator of the universe who arranged the stars, gave power to the sun and moon, and established the natural order. He communicates through the celestial bodies and natural phenomena, and all Pawnee ceremonies are ultimately directed toward him.
habitat: Above all—the highest heaven, beyond the stars
cultural_significance: The supreme being of the Pawnee, whose cosmic plan structures all of Pawnee religion, society, and ceremony.
summary: Supreme creator god of the Pawnee people who made the universe through the stars
fun_fact: Tirawa's creation involved the Morning Star fighting cosmic forces to mate with the Evening Star, producing the first human from their union

source: Wikipedia / Murie 1981

name: Atira
description: Atira is the Pawnee goddess of the Earth and wife of Tirawa, the creator god. Her name literally means 'Mother Corn,' and she is associated with the corn that sustained the Pawnee people. Atira is a nurturing figure who provides food and life from the earth. In the Hako (Calumet) ceremony, a symbol representing Atira was created, showing corn painted to represent the Rainstorm, Thunder, Lightning, and Wind. The South Bands of the Pawnee particularly honored Atira through agricultural ceremonies, giving thanks for the harvest and praying for continued fertility of the soil.
appearance: The Evening Star in Pawnee tradition, personified as a beautiful woman whose face shines with a soft, gentle light. She wears a robe of twilight purple embroidered with the first stars of evening, and her hair flows like the fading daylight.
behavior: The mother goddess who intercedes with Tirawa on behalf of humans. She receives the souls of the dead and guides them to the afterlife. She is associated with fertility, agriculture, and the nurturing aspects of the divine feminine.
habitat: The earth, cornfields, the Pawnee territory
cultural_significance: Atira is central to Pawnee agricultural ceremonies and represents the feminine, nurturing aspect of creation.
summary: Pawnee earth goddess and wife of Tirawa, associated with corn and fertility
fun_fact: Atira's name literally means 'Mother Corn' and she is honored in the Hako ceremony through a painted corn symbol representing the four storm forces

name: Evening Star
description: Evening Star is a female deity in Pawnee mythology, placed in the West by Tirawa. She initially resisted the divine plan to create humankind when Morning Star was sent to mate with her. Morning Star had to fight and defeat forces in the western sky to overcome her resistance. Their union produced the first human, a girl. Evening Star represents the feminine principle of creation, the western direction, and the mysteries of the night. In the Morning Star sacrifice ceremony, a captive girl was symbolically transformed into the Evening Star before her sacrifice.
appearance: A beautiful woman whose face appears in the western sky at sunset, wearing a gown woven from the colors of twilight. She is the mother of all stars and carries a baby star in her arms, which she nurtures until it is strong enough to shine on its own.
behavior: Mother of the stars who rules the night sky. She ensures the orderly passage of the stars across the heavens each night. She is a protector of women and children and is associated with the agricultural cycle and seasonal changes.
habitat: The western sky, the celestial realm
weaknesses: was overcome by Morning Star's power
cultural_significance: Evening Star's resistance and eventual union with Morning Star explains the origin of humanity in Pawnee cosmology.
summary: Pawnee goddess who became mother of humanity through union with Morning Star
